newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Hutu refugees show no apparent haste to quit Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Hutu refugees show no apparent haste to quit Zaire.

text.p: Rwandan Hutus trapped by Zaire's civil war have told U.N. refugee chief Sadako Ogata that they want a peaceful settlement to the conflict.
But with Tutsi-led rebels pushing the front ever closer, leaders of the 127,000 refugees clustered round this village showed no apparent haste to return home when she visited.
Ogata, however, told reporters travelling with her to Tingi Tingi on Saturday that this was the only solution as Zaire would not grant the refugees indefinite asylum.
"The refugees have to move out. They have to go back home but it is not clear how, when and on what conditions," she said, noting that the cheapest option was by road.
Ogata said the Zairean government and her UNHCR organisation had reached agreement on the principle of repatriating the remaining 300,000 or so Hutus.
She said the fast-moving front line posed a major threat to the refugees with the rebels taking Amisi, 70 km (45 miles) down the road to the east.
Tingi Tingi has the largest single grouping of refugees in eastern Zaire.
"I am appealing to those who have information about the frontline. I would like to...know what the impending danger is. It's a huge concentration of people," Ogata said.
Witnesses said refugees and Zairean villagers were moving west from Lubutu.
Innocent Seruntanga, who coordinates administrative matters in the Tingi Tingi area, said the refugees were panicking as the rebels captured more towns.
"The wind of panic is there. The war is getting nearer. Amisi is completely empty now," said Seruntanga.
The local governor, Omari Sisi, and a senior Zairean military commander confirmed the fall of Amisi.
Both sides confirmed fighting in the gold and tin mining town of Punia, deep in the forest, on another route south of Tingi Tingi.
A spokesman for the refugees, who fled with Hutu hardliners as rebels advanced in December, read a memorandum saying they were committed to a peaceful settlement. He did not elaborate.
Seruntanga predicted that hunger would force some Hutus to return to Rwanda but he added: "Only a tiny majority may be willing to return home."
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis by hardline Hutus in the former Rwandan army.
They fled west in December following attacks on their camps. Hundreds of thousands of fellow Hutus opted to return home in December, trekking en masse in the opposite direction.
Zaire, which accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of invading in support of the rebels, launched a much-touted counter-offensive on January 20.
The rebels hit back, advancing on fronts in the north, south and west of the border zone they control. Each side claims to have taken or retaken towns.
Relief agencies pulled their international staff out of Tingi Tingi and nearby Lubutu on Friday. Some returned on Saturday for Ogata's visit.

Witnesses said mutinous Zairean soldiers, demanding pay from relief agencies for pre-revolt work in refugee camps in the east, shot dead an officer who stepped in to stop a plan to take aid workers hostage.
"They went on a looting spree but that was quickly put down by well-disciplined soldiers," one aid official said.
Loyalists arrested 11 mutineers who were sent to Kisangani, headquarters of the counter-offensive, for trial.
Ogata later left for Kenya.
